A wean son WlNTalt.—We lave long had the feeling that Winter, in the main, has had but poor justice done him, both by eentimentalists and folks matter-of-fact enough. Certain analogists have finally net him down as the symbol of "Id age and death, thinking thereby tnat they have Settled the dear old fellow's destiny and ' position for all time. Not SO The keenest students ni Nature find in Ilint a mystery and a majesty which all the rosy colours and the most brilliant sunshine of the other seasons can never reveal Spring is dainty and sweet, hut tickle Summer is rich and Inecioue, but has a Delilah-like fascination—the siren's gift of sleep-giving song. Autumn—to the poet, as he thinks of the seasons —is sentimental and whining, in spite of Dill tinted garments and his spasmodic appeals to us nut., colour and song. We see, however, that his is a dying Inane, and that he has a hard struggle to keep even.flim- serf in good countenance, tie is, in fact, not sincere. nit lie leaves us with a pleading whine in his voice, and a departing message which we cannot but easociate with despondency. Not ei with Winter, however. He, tssi, has hri tender touches and sensibilities of the finest orders, only he does not niake them offensive to you by tor ever thrusting them into your presence. Fainter he is of the highest order; no sunsets, for matchless blue, ruddy tint, and ember bars, can match those of Winter, In all the rolling yaw. Sculptor he is too, and works with material whiter than marble, and to finer inues than ever were given to no in the masterpieces of Greece or Rome. Artist is he in all things, and that in the pendent and most dramatic order. What music is so esliiinn as hi, sts there rolls the breath of his hurri- cane through leagues of swaying pines, giving forth, to those who have the soul to listen, the sublimest psalms? —The Qifirt7 (..r February. There was the further consith•ration that it would be a breach of a sound rule in newspaper controversy to allow one correspondent to attempt to go behind the signature of another. But Mr. Thornton would not be saved from himself ;he urged that his letter should appear in full ; and, so rather than tisk misenncept ion, we left it to " Economist " to deter- mine—since he Woo the person Colleerned—wheth, the rule should be broken, and Mr. Thornton he given rope enough. ..,Je small borough of Newton returned two members to Parliament, and in the time of Charles I. these were Sir Miles Fleetwood and Sir Henry Edwards, knights. The extravagant demands of the King were refused, and he dissolved Parliament, but Newton sent the same two members again. Tie new Parliament was as obstinate in refusing the , demands of the monarch as the old one had been, I and was dismissed in a summary manlier, when Sir Ilenry Holcroft and Sir Francis Onslow secured the representation. But this new Parliament carried ; the celebrated •• Petition of Right,- and in its turn ,it was dissolved by the blindly wayward King. div.head: LAND NATIONALISATION.
div.p: LAND NATIONALISATION.

On Monday eyo..ning a lecture, under the anepices of the Land Not ionalisation Society, on " Land Nationalisation, was given in Wycliffe hall, War- rington, ie Councillor Threlfall, of Southport. In the absence through illness of Councillor Flood, Mr. T. Dian was elected to preside. There wan a good attendance, thORY on the platform, in addition to the Chairman and Lecturer, being Messrs. J. Salt, E. Wright, A. Riven, and S. Dunbobin. The CIiAIRSIAN said that land nationalisation ' was a very important subject and one which he thought was deserving of the most serious consider- ation of the working-classes of this country. as much consideration, positily, as any question that was at present agitating the public mind. tic: knew that there was a very great evil itt con- nection with the land and that it would nspiire some very strnnuoun efforts on their part to bring about a remedy. Hear, bear.) Ile then read a letter from Councillor Flood inwhich that gentleman wrote, "The question of the restoration of the land to the original possessors of the soil has brought into public review the gross robbery and wholesale con- fiscation that has swept away from off the land a race of men ,arnose descendants to-day art" swarm- in the midst of the greatest poverty arid wretched- ntss in our large centres of industry. The land system of England has been existing for ages for the benefit of the few at the expense of the many.' The Chairman also read an apology for non- attendance from Mr. John !Biding. Council" or THRIMFALI. then gave hia lecture. Tie said that during the last few years the idea or principle of the right of man has been driven home with greater force, and until the democracy nvognise the right ..f man and not the right of the landlord and not the right of the governing clanses alone—but the right of the very poor to a share of the wealth of this country, they could never hope for proper or wine government. They wanted to secure, as far as they could, for every man and woman in the country good find, decent clothing, and proper shelter, and they said that the first step to attain it mud be the securing of the land for tho people. riot of the things which had struck them during the last few ytars wan the overstoek.sl labour market, hut if the land tI the country were properly cultivated then, w, add be work for every one. Thelon,' question wan really at the root of all the depression and all their distress. The lecturer next refrrred to the very small proportion of England's popu- lation which is supported by the land, in compariem with the proportion similarly supp.rted in ether coun- tries and also to the great rise in agricultural rents whirli had taken place within the last hundred years.' With regard to the rents exacted for the use of land in I towns he mentioned that £90,000 a year wan drawn IT ! the noble duke who owned Covent Gan', in London, Nearly the whiten( this value )4 town land wan. pointed out, due to the indostry. enterprise and labour I of other people. Quoting from the evidence given before the Royal Commission ott the Housing of the Poor, Inc showed that in Variolls parts of London many of the labouring people iiild tO pay one-thinl, one-fourth and one-fifth of their incomes for single rooms to live in. In South - street, Pancras, as. a week was paid for one room, an underground kitchen was let at 2,13 d. per week, and ss. WaS paid for a single room in a state of great deray. In Spitalfields the average rental wash.; On. 6d. to Os. per week for one mon, and many of these tenements were referred to I by the Commissioners at instaneen of extreme over- crowding. Ile did not know how any I hivernment could, exist with facts like there before thein and go on I pottering atnut the iniquities prevalent in 'turmoil and other distant places. (Dear, !war and applause.) As another instance of the exaction of landlords, Mr Threlfall mentioned that when the Bootle Cor- poration, forced forward by inereaning trade, wished to extend their dock system they load to got,, Lord Derby who WA% the seecalled owner of the fore-shore and to make terms with hill], by which they had to pay him £200,000, the ratepayers of Bootle now paying £B,OOO a year as interest on that borrowed m.ey. (" Shame.") Dealing with various schemes of land reform, the lecturer said leasehold enfrinchinement might be a very good thing for the leaseholder, but they did not want to increase the number of property owners ; what they wanted was to secure to every inan a right lathe land of this country an that every man In the State might directly or indirectly weeive benefit from it. There would, he added, before long he an attempt to establish peasant proprietary. The simple reason for thin would lie that the cla,rtes were wise in their day and generation, and they knew that if they could create the landlord sprit in a larger number of people they would strengthen the rrnistance to any alteration in the present state of things. They maid that there was only one real remedy and that was nationalisation of the land.whielt meant that instead of, as at prenent, having individuals owning the land they would have the wholo of the land vented in the State. Mr. Threlfall then entered in some detail into a scheme whereby the land could be made public property through the medium of Municipalities, County Councils, and othor local authorities. The lecture was very attentively listened to and the lecturer was frequently and warmly applauded. Mr. Sexy moved "That this meeting is of opinion that no solution of the land question short of latal nationali- sation would be satisfactory to the people, and, in view of the decay of agrietiltiare, the growth of population, and the overstocked lalsair market, hereby calls upon Parliament to grant compulsory powers for the creation of small holdings in accordance with the principles of land nationalisation." That question of land nationalism- tion was, he said, one the importanco of which was second t.t none other. Ti.• tuvvial dintribution of wealth, which was the curs). of modern civilisation, Inc had seen traced to the institution of private property in land, and as long as that institution existed no increase in productive power could' permanently benefit the (Hear, hear.) .
Mr. llnnad.. in waalnding the motion, referred in particular to the question (of nwalties. Mr. E. Wl3lO. asked in what pcsition building societim would stand if land nationalisation was carried out?

Mr. TORVI.FALL replied that he odd that thotte people who had I 33 ght land should to emnponoam, and he, for ime, should be prepansl to say that in the case of building wrietiis they slemld be met with as liberal a compensation as the State tould allow. Mr. W. If.illreLF.l2 Said that, while agreeing with the lecturer and the motion, to woold like to ask whether Mr. Henry Georges' scheme id effecting the nationalis. ation of the land wax not simpler and better than that of the lecturer—that was to say by levying all taxes on land yahoo and ironing the taxes until almost the whole of the annual value itf the land was taken into the ctffers of the State.

Mr. 'l.ll 11E1,0.1. said that tin defeet id Mr. iieorge's scheme was that it was gradual while what was wanted wan a seheme that could la, speedily applitsl. Tin motion was then pot to tin ininiing and earrioil unanimously, and tin meeting terminated with a vote 'of thanks to the Chairman.

, Runcorn Croy Sessions, on Nlonday, before Mr. (1, L. Davies and Mr. Li. L. It igg, Henry Jack- son, landlord of the Wilson's Hotel, Bridge-st., was summoned for having. on the :loth January, UtrlttW- ifolly sold intoxicating liquor to George Connor and Frederick Findlay, during prohibited hours. Mr. I Cloirton. of Chester, prosecuted, on behalf of the police, and Mr. Robert Davies. of Warrington, defetnled.—inspeetor O'Donnell deposed that about midnight on the With January, he and l'.C. Ratcliffe went to the back of Wilson Ilotel. They got into the garden at tin' back of the h use. They went to the window of a room that opened on to the bowling green. The window blinds and curtains were drawn, but there was a space of two inches or more, at one corner, where they could see into the room. They noticed Mr. Connor, Mr. Findlay, and the landlord in the mini. They were sitting at a small table right opposite the window. Connor had a glass of beer before him, Findlay had spirits, and the landlord seemed to be drinking wine. About lialf- past twelve they had emptied the gla.ses, and the land- lord took them out ins a tray, and returned with them replenished. Mr. Connor put his hand int., hi, right hand trousers porket, and plarist Rune money in the landlord'. hand. The Inspector sent F.C. Ratcliffe for assistance, and knocked at the front deem. Ti..' landlord drank nit hid wine, and Mr. ('rumor ids beer, and they rise to their fist. Mr. Jackson left the room and closed the door after him, and the other two men looked round the room, and then also left the room. The back Jute being opened, the Inspector entered the house awl fitiind the persons concerned in the lobby. They nqurned into the room and the land- lord said he had no explanation to offer. "The own are here," he said. '` have been supplied, and have paid for it." Mr. Connor made a rambling statement that no drink hati 'wen supplied from 11 0. clock, aml they wenthillv waiting for a cab from Daresbury. At first Mr. Findlay ref ustsi to give his name,but afterwards did so, and said" Well, we have been supplied and have paid for our drinks.”—Mr. Davies t Vou have several times referred to" thew. men." I think you might have said gentlemen to persons in their position—lnspector O'Donnell : OIL yes ; I beg .your portion—Mr. Chasten It is more erslitable to be called a man than a gentle- man in the., days.—Mr. Davies It creates a watt of false imprexsitin.—ln reply to further questions, the Inspector said there was no disorder except that Mr. Connor was not sober.—P.C. Ratcliffe and l'.C. Bourne gave confirmatory testimony.—Mr. Davies said he apiatared not only for the unhtrtunate defendant, but also for Messrs. Greenall and Co., the pniprietors of the Hotel, which had afforded him shelter and refreshment twiny times in his life, and he was sorry to see the old toot' brought up on atteir a charge no this. Mr. Davies expressed astonishinent at the employwnt or Mr. Chins ton in such an A.B.C. care as this, and he should object to Mr. Jackson paving his fees. As the Bench had heard tlds was the day t;f the County C'ouncil election, and Mr. Connor arid Mr. Findlay were friends of Mr. harp, the successful candidate of the Danwbury They were sitting in the eommtqcial room waiting for the news of his victory, and for a tub to take the news to Weston. Asa matter of fart the news did not arrive unfit 10 minutes after the visit of the police. The house was quiet, they Were sitting in the proper place for men of their position, and thent was no attempt at eonceal- inent. Mr. Jackson did not think he WiLS breaking the law in allowing these gentlemen to wait for his trap ; and they were supplied with tire very moderate refreshment of a glass of beer anti two pennyworth of whisker. It was rather hard that on with a night as this,wlien evervbotly gave a littlelicentie, that this house should be spotted fort, trivial offence of this kind. Ile contended that Detre was no intention to break the law, and that the offence was merely technical, and as this wini the first offence, he thought the case might be dismissed on the payment of the costs of the ' police—Mr. Churton reinarked that the defendant was tined in 1884, and had been several limes suminoned.— Mr. Davies said that was five years ago. '('trio wag , 1/IPri•IV technical, and he aske.l the Bench, for the sake tit I the old house, for the sake of the man, Cu. the sake of : Runeorn, to dismiss the case.—Benjamin Jones, of Weston, deproßsl that Mr. Cemnor brought him the news of the election on the night its question.—The Bench. I after a brief retirement, said there was no doubt a breach of the law, but under the circumstances they had derided to impose a nominal fine of £3 and costs. The lieenso would not he endorsed.—ALr. Csinnor and Mr. Findlay were then chargisi with being on ficensed prerinses during prohibited hours,and they pleaded guilty. Mr. F.. Wynne Humphreys addressial ' the magistrates on their behalf, and said he could pre duce Mr. harp to prove that the gentlemen were to take the result of the election Cr, Weston at his request. The order Woo given for the cab early in the afternwtri. The result of the poll should have arrived at the hotel at half- past ten, but Mr. Jackson's son,who was driving the trap, stayed at the request of several police constables to give them a lift, With the result that Mr. Connor anti Mr. Findlay were kept waiting. They were not in the house for the purpose of drinking. The Inspectorhail suggested they went drunk, but he knew sufficient of the Inspector's character and reputation in Ow.. rases to know that if any charge of drunkenness could have been made he would only have Men too glad to take out a summons against them. The charge against them wt. even less than that against the landlord, and setis merely teehnical. —The Bench finedeach defendant 100, and costs BA. Bd.

Pr eight days ' before the thane of Commons net again, lint he ...bid not find it in his heart to go away without coming to see his friends at Runeorn —•applausi•i—a• seei n g all that might in. gathered in that buililing,as he knew tin-re was not room for them all there. (Ltughter.) Ile mil. gratulated them most heartily utmn the work done in Cheshire within the laqt monfh. (Hear, hear.) If they recollected that Che,bin. was repre,ented in Parliament by two Liberals and eleven Conservatives, and then Consii•lenssf that in the County Council then • were as many Liberals as Conservatives. and three gentlemen who would probably vote with the Liberals. they could see what a wonderful change had cony- over Cheshire during the last three ymrs. I Floe, hear.) Ile knew one or two gentlemen who win' descritaid us Liberal ['Monists, who were to 114' a phrase that had become popular in Leitidon,—good inunieipal Liberals ; and as such they were in their right place on the County Council. He must congratulate them upon the fact that the Liherat representative of Rune•irn showed himself in his true colours entire pnivions day (applause). and he had to thank the meeting for rewarding trim for the work that night. (Hear, hear.) Ile must tell them frankly that in Runeorn they hail bungled matters. (Hear, hear, and applause ; A Voice : 't not the smrkingi class population." Applause.) But allow hitn to MI them that the manner in which they saw the state of affairs is the best of all auguries for the future. (Hear. hear.) He know that the mistakehaying been made,they had made up their minds manfully that it should never Ire made again applause.) Ile saw More iliM the person of Mr. Benjamin liniveton, a man who had done a grand, work in the RildisbUrypivision. Hear, hear,. When I they found there were SIN stout Radicals returned in the County Council for the Eddishury Dimsion, they knew whom to thank for it. (Hear, hear.) They had seen I too what wonderful work hail been done by the Libentls and Radii-ale of London. London had been the great difficulty of Liberals. and -he thought they might very well tale heart and hope'and look forwaid with cheer. huh courage to the next general election as far as London was roneerned. (Hear, hear.) The sooner they had general election and the better. Hear. hear.) In his opinion it wasthe duty of the Liberals of this country to rail upon the leaders of the Liberal party, one and all, to do everything in their power to bring about a din solution a Parliament at the earliest possible moment. (Applause.) It seemed to him that at tho present time, whentlieCnnservativeliovernment were bringing absolute

.. shmne anon the name of Englishmen,it was trietiutytif the Liberal party to take every legal and constitutional I means to bring that state of things to an end. (Applause.) They had a number of gentlemen in the I . House of Commons that blocked the way. They got , patted on the back by the Tot 7 party every week, and the flattery they received in the House of Commons would turn honest men's stomachs--(laughter)--but I they swallowed it all, and what was to he done with them he did not know. A proposition had been made that the Liberals in all eonstituencies represented by I Unionists should sign a requisition calling moon them to resign. Ile was veto muelt afraid that they would have , their trouble for thrir pains, if they did. But Inc (Mr. Brunner) had a duty to iart on in the House of (ton. mons as their representative, and lie wanted to go back fortified with their authority that when he sass- a chance of doing anything whatever within the lines of the con- stitution to turn this Government out, that he asked their authority to do it. t Loud applause.) He did nit think that after that expression of feeling, he need take • formal vote upon the subject. (Applause.) Mr. W. Handley had drafted a re:solution by which they might express their opinion upon certain pliases of the present , political situation, and he had no doubt it would meet with their hearty appnwal. (Applause.) Mr. E. IVI•oar thistruttrxs moved •• That this meeting , strongly protests atrainst the pre,ent cruel artd inhuman method of governing Ireland : and the barbarous treat- ment of her chosen representatives by the so-called Unionist Government and pledges itself to support our member J. T. Brunner, Esq., and our honoured leader the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, in their efforts to obtain equal laws and liberties with ourselves for our fellow-subjects in that unhappy country:' (Applause.) Mr. 8.1.1.AVY seconded the resolution, which was sup- ported by Mr. JEFFS, and carried unaniniously. The meeting terminated with the usual votes of , thanks.

But what of his programme i' Two of its Vim, items,Free Education, and the improvement of the condition of the Centers, are already planks in the platform tif the Liloeral party; and astothe tirade proposal to keep Open Purse bar Landlords, under pretence of doing something for the tenants, we venture to prellict that it is as bubble that will burst even whilst it is being examined. As regards Free Education, it is just possible that there may he here and there an isolated supporter of the mein- her for West Birmingham who will conclude that, in bringing this subject to the fr. nit, he is return- ing to his old love. But it is his inlil love with a new face. It lam not hitherto been stipposed that in advocating Free Education he wan prepared to ' carry it out by further endowing denominational sells nit. Vet this is what his plan comes to as presented at Glasgow. Hu says .-- The religious question is left eat inly where it is by my proposal. The suggestion which I make is that a compulsory tax which is now levied upon the parents at a certain period of their existence should in f mum be levied on the whole taxation of the country, to which the parents, of course, con- tribute so well as everybody else. How any man calling himself a Radical, and still preaching the doctrine of religious equality, can bring himself to make such a proposal is to us utterly inconcoviable, except on the supposition that he has made up his mind, SIDCO he cannot " run," tt i try to "ruin " the Liberal party. Mr. 1 ' CHAMDSSLAIN would have us believe that this is the view he has always Liken of the question ; and refers amazed inquirers Vi au article in the 4` Fortnightly Review," published a few years ago under his responsibility. To that article, we have not at this nioment access, list we have access to the 1,14111410 known as "'rue Radical Programme," also palatial.' meter Mr, CHAMBERLAIN'S responsibility : and there is not a word in tie chapter on Free Seleals to suggest that he was prepared to make such a base I surrender. It leis always been understood amongst j attend Radicals that, whenever edacation w;:s I made free, primary schools, sapport,tl either by taxes or rates, lie both, would be got , by elected representatives of the taxpayers or ratepayers. It is the corner stone of municipal government that those who find the , money shall control its expenditare ; anal " The , Radical Programme " supports this view ; for MI 1 palm 177 we find it stated that--" As a matter inf 1 , fact the law is administered not in the interests of education, parents, children, Or ratepayers, last in ElloBo if doIIiiIIIIIISEIRIIIII 10100114... How RIM Free Schools bets.se a remedy for tins defect, if Mr. CHAMBERLAIN makes laid worse by adding to the funds which are contonlled by uncontrolled managers l But page 206 of "'rite Radical Pro- 1 gramme" speaks out, MOM emphatically, as follows:

All this want of sympathy and en-operation, which gives the teacher slum an men ill tight, would he remedied if the parents had lull proprietary rights i in the schools, if they were mien without budge or ticket, and if they were in is larger degree under their own control and the management of their own class. 6' Under their own control and the management of their own class --what can that mean, if it does not mean that, with Free Education, slusil mau- -1 goes are to become the representatives of the ratepayers? Mr. CHAMBERLAIN now Beast° ignore this vital principle; and is ready to play hit-, the hands of the clerical party in ardor to steal a march upon the Liberals. Like the Tories with whom be is now allied, it would seem he can " turn and twist mid change every full moon."

Ma. BALFOUR finds that he cannot "dismiss the topic" of the prison treatment of Mr. o.l3spui in the airy style which he adopted at the Dublin : banquet. No small portion of that speech was , devoted to the matter, aid he has since had to follow it up with a long letter of explanation and , defence. Unfortunately for the limn SECRETARY, he explains nothing and he defends nothing. He calls attention with a flourish of trumpets to the , following passage in Mr. Miami's criminal speech as "his real offence," and not the passage which the member for County Cork himself quoted,—" I iun afraid land-grabbers are living and thriving in the midst of you. If all our labours for the last ten years have not been in! vain, you itight to know bow to ileal with land- , grabbers." This is the little mouse which the epistolatory mountain in labour has brmight forth. , But this extract merely hints at boycotting, while ass matter of fact Mr. O'BRIEN advocated boy - eating initright --on the lines if the Primrose mLeague. Ile is the champion .4 slink " butcher of his district, i and, on Wednesday, at the Manchester Police Court, secured the distinction of haying his name , attached, not to is imel4l —but to a penalty of £lOO. Magistrates do not as a rule properly appreciate talents of the Albert Hoyle class. What is is hun- dred shillings to a Mall of his stamp But £loo— is something like.

The Rev. F. Slater, of Latchford, speaking in St. : James's Schoolroom, on Monday evening, said 1" smile ladies bad remarked they never knew people so hard to get to church as m Warrington." Can it be that people's tastes are in the direction of the spiritinom rather than the spiritual if no, the clergy would do well to try to cripple the influence of Sir Gilbert GreenalLinstead of adding .to it. Free-and-easy worship of God and Mass- moo is the reverse of edifying. - An wee to he expected, the directors of the Manchester Ship Canal Company had a favour- able report to present to the general mooting of shareholders, which was held in Manchester on Monday. The work goes merrily forward; that is patent to everylsaly ; and there is reason now to believe not only that the undertaking will be com- pleted, but that it will be finished within the stipulated time. As the chairman prettily said, it is not 110 W a question of faith bit of works.

The tHadstonian programme, in which . Inland ,i•od in the forefront, would, however. bear examinat in. Some if those who now criticised it were amongst its authors. awl he could not help but : wonder why they now cril Wised it insteadot helping it. ' Ti,,, Irish question was taking a new aspect. There was a rising tide of feeling in lltvat Britain which meant that Englishmen were roused to the realities of the misrule in Ireland. They saw that the pieotre unrolled before them was one which offended the very instincts of free men, and conflicted with all that was beg in the history of English institutions and English laws. Soon this moment the only distinction between politiciallS in Eng- land vom thedistinetion between Coercionists and Anti- Coercionists, and for the present he accepted no ..then distraction.--Speaking at Portsmouth on Thursday, Mr. Morley said the twospiwts of next session were not. very exhilarating, Isvatew they were about to spend a groat deal of money, while they would have very little legisla- tion. Ile admitted that it R 11.4 necessary to improve the national defences, and, touehing on Mr. Chamberlain's challenge to publish the pr. weedings of the Round Table Conference, he said the Liberal party would lose nothing by thin pour.; being bilte.n.

div.p: THE AUSTRIAN TRAGRDY.

.• Truth " says: -We have not got to the bottom, it appears, of the Meyerling tragedy. Before there was time to concoct a good circumstantial account I that would hold well together the official people , blurted out that Rudolph Was shot behind ths ear in a diagonal direetion, and that the coronet part of the skull was carried off by the ball as it went out of the head. Nothing at all was said of Marie Ter- I where. We might fancy that it was she who I discharged the pistol. if As had not been shot in the back. Both were found dead on the same coach, and there were farm scattered upon Marie. Does not this point to a woman's band, to a maniac from jealousy, and to irony in vengeance? The diagonal shot upwards also points to somebody having been concealed in the room, under a bed or a table or some other piece of furniture, and creeping along stealthily until he or she got up to the sleeping ' pair, and placing the muzzle of the pistol elm, to Rudolph's head, and tiring up at it. Marie would ! doubtless, on hearing the shot, have sought to have jumped out. when she was knocked over by a I pistol shot in the back. There were mutilations also, it appears, of both bodies,which showed mani- ' acal hatred. The hypothesis of a double murder is everywhere accepted out of England. Some imagine that the shots must have been tired by the brother of a young princess, others by a gamekeeper, and then there is the theory of an illustrious personage having lain in ambush under the tattle until the lovers were asleep. But the curious thing is that everyone (out of England) thinks it all right that an heir apparent to a dual empire should have been shot because he was en bonne fortune. The tendency on the Continent is to keep down gallantry by granting impunity to kill those who are caught.

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN IN SCOTLAND.
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN IN SCOTLAND.

Mr. and Mrs. Chamberlain and Mr. Austen Chamber- lain arrived in Glasgow on Monday night. They were mat by Mr. Alexander Cross, who drove them to lila house, where they dined. Abent 11 o'clock they attended a eenverwstione in the St. Andrea's Halls, which were crowded with a fashionable company. Addresses were presented to Mrs. Chamberlain from Hie ! Women's, Liberal Unionist Associations. Mr. Chamber- lain, in reply, expressed hearty thanks on behalf of I himself and wife for the kindness and welcome extended ' 1,, them in Scotland. He pmeeeded to speak upon the Irish question, and contended that the rase of the United States gave no sanction to the claim of Home , Rule on the lines I d Mr. Gladstone's Bill. On Tuesday night Mr. Chamberlain addressed a ' crowded meeting in St. Andrew's hail, Glasgow. Letters were read from Lord Hartington and Sir Henry James. Mr. Chamberlain. in his speech, referred to what he !described as the Clerkenwell-cum-Limehouse prot,rranime set up by Mr. Gladstone merely as a kind of politieal birdlime aground bait. When Mr. Gladstone had the opportunity of ineluding the one man one vote principle' I in his Reform Bill he had refused to do to, although urged privately in that direction by his OVII col- leagues. They eould not be sure either of his views ,as to Disestablishment. The Liberal Unionists were I determined to resist his Irish itelicy as danger- I ous.dn the best interests of the natio-in. The lesson , of the elections at Govan and elsewhere ws' I that the English people had determined to put aside , , the Irish question as an unnecessary interruption to the ! continued stream of progress going on in this country. ! The Unionists should now give to the enuntry a con- structive policy, and among the items which he would suggest were tree education, the extension of the Land Purchase Act, and the measure of relief for the crofters of Scotland. SpeakinF, 14 Mr. Gladstone's flame Rule I measure for Ireland, he said the bill was dead by the I common consent of its parent and of all its suppoiters. Mr. Gladstone refuses, he declared, to put before as his views, in spite of constant requests, and he (Mr. I Chamberlain) believed he was not in a position to do so. Mr. rhaenberlain was the guest of the Glasgow Litte- red Club on Wednesday night, In respnmiing to the toast of his health, he said no one would morn gladly welcome the re-union Id the Liberal party than he would. The difference between them arose on only nne branch of the Irish question ; on other branches they were practically agreed, and there was also unanimity in regard to Scotch reforms which were now ripe for settlement. Ile appealed to the Glad.stonian Libe- rals to press forward those reforms on which all were agreed, and to put in the background the sole question on which they were not united. and he invited his colleague; at the " Round Table. Confer- ence " to publish what occurred at their meetings rela- tive to the Irish land question, because he believed good , would arise from it. He expressed regret that theism- penance party neglected to avail itself of the opportunity , of legislation on licensing matters afforded by the Loral I Government Bill. Finally, he expressed confidence that . the passionate hatred of 'asset which had always anima- ted the Lateral party would outlive the temporary I differences, and enable the party to continue the per- vading influence in the destinies of the country. On Thurslav night Mr. Chamberlain, spoke in Dundee. Dealing with Mr. O'Brien's ease, the right lion, gentle- mass denied that his mass political offenee, for there was no such thing under the Crimes Act. Mr. O'Brien had , been committed for using language which experience I showed had in previous cases been followed by outrage and assassination.

An open-air anti-coercion demonstration by the Radical electors of Dundee was held the same evening. The meeting took place in Albert Square, and was attended be nearly 40,000 persons. Prior to the mieaking an effigy of Mr. Chamberlain, who was addressing a meeting in Rinnaird Hall, wan burst, amidst great cheering. Revolt, thins were passed condemning the cruel treatment of Mr. O'Brien, denouncing Mr. Chamberlain as a political renegade, and calling for the immediate grunt of Home Rule to Ireland. The meeting dispersed in an orderly manner, after giving cheers for Mr. Gladstone and Mr. O'Brien

div.head: COOKING MADE EASY.
div.p: COOKING MADE EASY.

To get your joint, or your fowl, is one thing, and to cook it is another. The culinary process, as ordinarily carried oasis one that is beset with many , difficulties, and a good cook is usually esteemed as a treasure. What stein must he said of the recent invention that bids fair to bring about a revolution in cookery? The Waltzer " lamp and cooker, the invention in question, is to outward seeming a simple apparatus, but it i”aid that Mr. Waltzer, of sewing machine fame, the inventor, has been think.ing over it, and experimenting with regard to it, for about fifteen years. The cooking apparatus proper , consists primarily of a shallow copper dish, which is placed over the heat generator, and contains about a pint of water. This pint of water converted into steam represents the amount of heat power (about five and a half times the nominal heat of boiling water) requisite to cook a plain dinner of slob, meat, and vegetables sufficient for a family of six or eight persons. rir cylinder of block tin, with a door in the side, is placed in the dish so that the base stands in the water. In this cylinder, twllei the corking drum, are arranged, one above .other, the tin dishes (earh of which fits into its place) containing the (+wed which it is desired to cook. Over the whole is then placed a second larger cyclinder with a solid lid, the low end of winch also stands in the I water, thus rendering air-tight the whole apparatus I which it enduses. Heat being then applied, the water I is, in the fractional part a a minute, converted into steam, which rises through the inner cyclinder, or cook- ing drum, entirely surrounding and enveloping the food, until it reaches the top of the condenser, when it is cooled and condensed into moisture, which passes to the bottom of the vessel, to be teconvertwl into steam. This regenerati, process goon on on inflailem, and as there is no escape for the steam, or iso necessity arises for replenishing the water supply or indeed for interfering in any way with the amwratus from the moment that the food is placed in it until it is ready to come to table. The apparatus is automatic in its scram, and err rho a dinner without any watching being nsluired. There is no eswape of steam or odours, Ow food cannot tw burned or smokes', and it is claimol that if dinnsr happens to be delays,' for an hour or so it may be left to gr. on strain- ing with the certainty of not being.. spoilt. ESononty is another advantage gained, for the Cooker below, masts, fries, stews, and steams at a owt of "yea than half a farthing an hoar, and for lows than one halfpenny a dinner for eigh p t eople can la- retiredio a state of per- ' foliar. The lamp burning paraffin oil which supplies the heat can be twwl separately for illuminating purposes • and it hasthe great merit IA being absolutely non-explo- sive ; it can even be rolled about Mc floor when lighted, with perfect safety. On Monday a representative of • the Examiner " was present at a testing Won at Whitefield, near Manchrato and had the opportunity of sraing a number of the Cookers perform- ing tlieir work. :\ bout fie Vof the gentlemen who were present at the exhraition clt dywn to adiemer I, Poked by the Wauser Stoves,and there,. a concensus of opinion that the various dishes c• sad nat pissibly have been better cotkol. The now;invent ion. in addition to being no useful in the hotosffi, +l,l,is invaluablersn an arcearary to camping roar" nrrnd picnic parties, as it is portal ile, and ; can be carried ah,ait wrnln perfect safety and very little trouble. It 1)13y with truth iv old that by the + invention of the Wanaor Cooker and Lallip another ° long felt scorn' has been supplied. We understand that the inakers have enterod into arrangements with , Mr.]. S. shirt:rad, of Bridge-st., Warrington, to act as ' their local agent.

div.p: THE PEACEFUL DEMOCRACY Dv_ v..sm.

The rapid advance of science in recent years, while alleviating hi many ways the sufferings of men, has also wondennisly added to their power of indicting serious and lasting injury to each other. The knowledge of good has, in this case, carried with it tile knowledge of evil. Mans increased control over the forces of nature may be used to a good or a had end from whence it appears tlmt purely secular education, unaccompanied by moral training, is scarcely desirable. Nowhere is the power with which science has armed man more strikingly shown than in the latest appliance of modern warfare •tire Zalinski Pneumatic Gun. This formidable weapon of destruction is adapted to throw shells containing from Ita) lbs. to 300 Ilm. of 75 per cent. dynamite, over a distance of 2,000 , yards. The sir pressure required is about 1.000 lb.. I per square itieh, and the experiments made by the American Government well the 15 inch guns I intended for the new dynamite cruiser. Testivitia have been fairly satisfactory. Tire" Daily News" correspondent sends a graphic account of the pro- ceedings. The tirst shot was made with WOlbs. of the explosive substance. There WILA a sharp report, and then a long black object was seen flying throligh the air. It mounted gradually till it reached a height of about one hundred feet, and then began to curve towards the water. It was about eighteen seconds in the air before it touched the water and disappeared, and a Seeollll afterwards a huge majestic pyramid of foaming water arose from 15Oft. to 200 ft. into the air, making a most gorgeoua spectacle as it was lighted by the rays of the afternoon eon. A shell containing a much larger amount of explosive was then used, the eleva- tion being much gnmier, and the size of the projectile was seen Sr lie enormous no it rose nearly ' Rat feet. But it then began to turn over in the air, twisted about (sits course, and finally tumbled.. point foremost, into the water 450 yards short of the mark. It explod, d almost instantly, sending a tremendous volitme of water hundreds of feet into the air, with such violence that no vessel could have escaped destruction withia a radius of a hundred feet A few snch shells t brown int o Liverpool would slim:lily reduce that •stately city to rides. Modern warfare is fast becoming a inatter of chemists and ' engineers. The ,lays are gone when strong men wrestled face to face, and foes locked in deadly embrace died in each other arms. Opportunities for feats of valour, such as the poets sing of, are few: and a thousand able inen may be ruthlessly n mow down without their ever obtaining a glimpse of the cause which no hurriedly transforms them from living, thinking men, into shapeless and bloody objects. The latest idea in torpedoes—that of a Russian officer is grim in the extreme. The boat is directwl by a solitary individual who, in blowing up the enemy's vessel, annihilates himself. This may open away for individual bravery; but the I certainty of one's being converted into a cloud of "red mould," in the course of a few seconds, can hardly be regarded with complacency by a vast majority of men. It is (Luke possible that "Armed peace," a j favourite idea of Bismarck's, will be the only work- able alternative to wasting warfare for some genera- tions to come. International Arbitration is good, and demands the advocacy of every true patriot; its buainess is to educate men for the future. But for the present we must take men as we find them; and while it may be considered patriotic to dispute Carlyle's cynical statement that most are 'mostly feols," yet it can hardly be denied that men are led oftener by their prejudices and desires than they are by the cool calculations of reason. As with men wi with nations : first the natural, after- wants t hat which is spiriival. The advance in the methods of scientific warfare will lay an increasing burden upon the shoulders of responsible statesmen -a burden winch will certainly lead them to con- sider with becoming gravity any steps leading to what would inevitably be an appalling destruction of life and property. Still, statesmen are only num, and often ambitious and out of touch with the people, and the fact remains that the lives and property of millions of European citisens are in the , hands of kalf-a-dosen men playing the usual matic game of skill and cunning. Twenty-eight million able-bothed men are ready to take up arms on the next outbreak of European hostilities. The condition of Europe is certainly not calculated to induce feelings of security; the continued improve- ments in quick-firing guns, and the elaborate arrangements for the rapid mobilisation and con- centration of troops tend to confirm the opinion that the next war will result in little less than race extermination. It is in the direction of the democracy we mist look if we are, humanly speaking, to have a faith in a coming day when lire" Nations shall learn war I no more." In the growth of democratic power will Ire found the force which shall ultimately cause the horrors of war to be a thing of the past, to lie wondered at -an awful dream gone on the wings of Eternal Night before the risen Sun of Liberty and Righteousness. It is rather too late in I the day for Lord Wolseley to advocate conscription with any reasonable hope of gaining the enrol the country. If lie wished to render himself conspicu- ous he has admirably succeeded ; iris rampant militarism has placed hitn in an unspeakably fool- ish position. The people of thin country are uot going to have continental necessities imported here, even to please Lord Wolseley. Statesmen and Generals are too often inclined to look upon the masses of their fellows as or, many units to be fed, governed, or led to slaughter as the cane may be, but the people look upon the questions affecting their welfare in quite a different way. As they advance, the power of Princes' wanes, diplomatic jugglers sue for mercy, commerce revives and peace scatters the fair traits of plenty over the land. And it may be that in the years to come, I when the advance of scientific warfare has ren- dered it possible for a nation to be annihilated in a few days, a counterbalancing development of nobler aspirations, sentiments and feelings shall have secured the impossibility of such a ruthless slaughter ever taking place. But this depends upon the continuance of religion, not as a thing of creeds, but as a code of life and duty.

The seventh ordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the Manchester Ship canal Com- pany was held on Monday, in St. James's Hall, Manchester. There was a large attendance. Lord Egerton of Tatton, the chairman of the company, presided. The report states that at the last half-yearly meeting the shareholders were advised that it would be necessary to seek authority from them Ito borrow 43,000,000 early in October. This was rendered unnecessary by the promptness with I which the call due on the 12th September was met, by the large sum paid in advance of future calls, and in consequence of the estimate of expen- diture in land and works being in excess of require- ments. An extraordinary meeting of the company will be held at the conclusion of the half-yearly meeting to authorise the exercise of the borrowing powers of the company to the amount of ii,ar.wou. div.p: LAN6.ISIIIRE COUNTY COUNCIL

The second meeting of the Provisional Council (provisional till it takes over the management of affeurs in April) 0101 held on Thursday in the County I Hall at Predon. .Ilr. Alderman J. T. Rilibert, the provisional chairman, presided. There were 129 of the lift inembers present. The Hight Hon. .1. T. Haden was elected Chairman for the ensuing year. Mr. Hibbert ment lotted that under the old system I of county government tire fottrteen committees consisted of 310 members, whereas the County Council was a body of only 140,consequently lie was afraid they would be rather hard worked. It moat he remembered that there were fourteen county boroughs in Lancashire, with a population of 1.5110,0X1, against LfOlOti in the county proper: and a rateable, value of .e.1,7011,0(110, against J:5,900,1aa I. Mr. C. It. Jocson was afterwards elected vice-chairman, and considerable controversy ensued I regarding the composition of a committee to confer with the Committee of County Justices appointed by the Court of Anneal Session. Alderman E. K. Muspratt urged that the County Council committee charged with the duty specilieel should consist of gorlemen who were not 3mstices, seeing that the latter were on well represented on other committees. Several members objected to the principle of reject- ing a man because he was a magistrate, and ulti- mately Alderman NI tops= withdrew his motion. The Committee was ultimately composed as fol- tows :—The Chairman and the Vice Chairman ex- officio. Lancaster T. Preston, James Ashworth. West Herby: T. Hughes, Colonel Meat% .I. Mercer, T. Snape, F. Monks Warrington I,J. Unwin. Pre. ton: T. Lightbown, 11. Maden, ffev. 1.. O. Wood, 11. Haweliffe. Salford V. K. Armitage, G. 11. Gaeldum, A. Forrest, J. Fletcher, J. C. Mather. and J. C. Need- ham.- -The following gentlemen were appointed a comtnittee to draw up Standing Orders for the Council: -J. Fell, G. 11. Cadelum, M. W. Peace, E. Cross, It. Aasheton, T. Preston, E. K. Muspratt, J. U. Needham, T. Snape. with the Chairman and Vice Chairman--This High Sheriff's return of the election expenses was laid upon the table. The ' total amount was .T 3,753. There had been 36 con- tested elections, 47 uncontested, and 13 members were returned by boroughs. It wine agreed to print the proceedings of the Council fer the convenience of the members. —Mr. Alderman Fitxterbert-Broek- holes gave notice that he would move for the appointment of a committee to consider the best manner of dealing in future with ponsionsand sweet- , animation allowances.- --Mr. John• White ( Warring- I ton), asked a question with regard tollie principle , 011 which aldermen would be elected in future. in [he care, say, of a vacancy.- Mr. Alderman pratt said that the principle adopted, at the last meeting would not he binding, but it showed the t feeling of the majority of the members on the sub- jeet.—This was all the business. The next meeting i of the Council will be held on March 14..
